Holographic Quantum Transformer: A Generalist Neuro-Symbolic Architecture for Solving Frustrated Systems via Generative Attention

Conference: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2; August 09–13, 2026; Jeju Island, Republic of KoreaProceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2 (KDD ’26), August 09–13, 2026, Jeju Island, Republic of KoreaDOI: 10.1145/3770855.3818932ISBN: 979-8-4007-2259-2/2026/08CCS: Computing methodologies Neural networksCCS: Applied computing PhysicsCCS: Computing methodologies Machine learning

Abstract.

Simulating two-dimensional frustrated quantum matter is a grand challenge due to the sign problem and exponential Hilbert space complexity. In this work, we introduce the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT), a physics-inspired generative architecture that leverages global self-attention to resolve non-local entanglement patterns. We validate HQT on the square lattice J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg model. On the heavily frustrated 8×88\times 8 lattice at the quantum critical point (J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5), HQT reaches a ground-state energy per site (E/NE/N) of −0.5001​(𝟏)\mathbf{-0.5001(1)}, consistent with the expected finite-size scaling trend. Beyond numerical accuracy, HQT exhibits intrinsic physical awareness, autonomously recovering the underlying J2J_{2} interaction geometry through interpretable attention maps. Our central contribution is “Holographic Transfer", a zero-shot size-extrapolation protocol with rapid alignment: a model trained on 8×88\times 8 systems is directly projected onto larger 10×1010\times 10 lattices via continuous positional-embedding interpolation and head re-initialization, achieving high-fidelity initialization and rapid convergence. This zero-shot protocol yields an energy of E/N=−0.49782​(𝟑)E/N=\mathbf{-0.49782(3)}, statistically consistent with the variational state of the art while requiring no from-scratch training on the target lattice. Our results establish generative attention as a scalable paradigm for transferable quantum simulation.

Keywords: 
Neural Quantum States, Transformer, Frustrated Magnetism, Transfer Learning, Quantum Phase Transition, Variational Monte Carlo, AI for Science.

1. Introduction

As originally envisioned by Feynman (Feynman, 1982), simulating quantum physics with classical computers faces an exponential barrier: the Hilbert space dimension grows as 2N2^{N}. While quantum hardware has made strides in error mitigation (AI, 2023), verifiable advantage on practical many-body problems remains limited. Consequently, classical simulation algorithms continue to serve as the primary engine for discovery.

However, traditional numerical methods encounter fundamental barriers in two-dimensional (2D) frustrated systems. Tensor Network methods like PEPS and DMRG (Wang et al., 2016) are constrained by the Area Law of entanglement (Eisert et al., 2010), limiting simulations to narrow cylinders. Conversely, Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC), the workhorse for unfrustrated systems, hits a hard wall in frustrated regimes (e.g., the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model) due to the “Sign Problem”. As proven by Troyer and Wiese (Troyer and Wiese, 2005), solving the generic sign problem is NP-Hard. Although recent solvers by Nomura and Imada (Nomura and Imada, 2021) have established high-precision benchmarks, a general polynomial-time solution remains elusive.

The intersection of AI and Physics has sparked a paradigm shift. Carleo and Troyer (Carleo and Troyer, 2017) pioneered Neural Quantum States (NQS) using Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs). As reviewed by Dawid et al. (Dawid et al., 2025), deep networks have shown remarkable capacity to represent complex wavefunctions.

Early NQS architectures, such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) (Choo et al., 2019), exploited local correlations. However, as noted in very recent work by Li et al. (Li et al., 2025), CNNs struggle to capture global topological order due to limited receptive fields. To address sampling bottlenecks, Sharir et al. (Sharir et al., 2020) introduced deep autoregressive models, and Hibat-Allah et al. (Hibat-Allah et al., 2020) applied Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). While efficient, RNNs impose an artificial 1D bias on 2D lattices (Medvidović and Moreno, 2024).

The field is evolving rapidly towards global architectures and theoretical rigor. Theoretical works have linked deep networks to quantum entanglement (Levine et al., 2019; Deng et al., 2017), while equivariant networks (Luo et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2024) incorporate physical symmetries. Recently, Nomura (Nomura and Imada, 2025) solidified NQS for strongly correlated electrons, and Liu et al. (Liu et al., 2025) explored advantages on photonic platforms.

Crucially, the Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al., 2017) has emerged as a powerful tool. Viteritti et al. (Viteritti et al., 2023) and Sprague et al. (Sprague and Czischek, 2024) demonstrated that attention mechanisms can resolve frustrated states. However, most existing approaches are “instance-specific”: a model trained on a small lattice cannot generalize to larger ones. While transfer learning has been explored (Zen et al., 2020; Westerhout et al., 2020), and recent studies investigate scaling laws (Knitter et al., 2026) and sample complexity (Rouzé and França, 2024), a unified framework for Zero-Shot Size Extrapolation with Rapid Alignment is missing.

Our Contribution: The Holographic Quantum Transformer. Theoretical insights from Swingle (Swingle, 2012) suggest a duality between entanglement renormalization and holography. We posit that the Transformer’s attention is the computational realization of this principle. We propose the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT) (Figure 1), a neuro-symbolic architecture designed to crack frustrated systems. Our contributions are:

  1. (1)

    Holographic Encoding: Building on the duality proposed by Swingle, we explicitly interpret the self-attention matrix as a Holographic Entanglement Map, capturing long-range correlations that define topological order.

  2. (2)

    Generative Autoregression: We implement an autoregressive sampling scheme that guarantees exact normalization and zero autocorrelation, overcoming the sampling limitations of traditional MCMC and enabling efficient exploration of the Hilbert space.

  3. (3)

    Geometric Deep Learning Paradigm: We demonstrate that global attention, when augmented with our continuous positional embeddings, outperforms the local receptive fields of CNNs in capturing topological defects. This establishes HQT as a geometric deep learning framework capable of resolving non-local structures on grid manifolds.

  4. (4)

    Effectively Mitigating the Sign Problem: By injecting geometric inductive biases, we effectively navigate the rugged energy landscape of the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model at the highly frustrated point, effectively mitigating a problem known to be NP-hard for classical stochastic methods.

  5. (5)

    Zero-Shot Size Extrapolation with Rapid Alignment: Inspired by the scaling laws of 2025 (Knitter et al., 2026), we introduce a “Projection Re-initialization” transfer protocol. This allows our model to learn the universal syntax of the Hamiltonian on small lattices and generalize to large-scale systems without retraining, moving toward a transferable, size-generalizable quantum simulator.

While recent works have explored neural quantum states and transfer learning, our approach introduces distinct physical priors. Unlike methods like FLIP that target Parametrized Quantum Circuits (PQCs) on actual quantum hardware, HQT operates in the classical Neural Quantum States (NQS) domain. Furthermore, while standard sequence NQS architectures (e.g., Viteritti et al. (Viteritti et al., 2023)) flatten the lattice into 1D sequences and require training from scratch per size, our core novelty lies in the Holographic Mapping. By explicitly injecting 2D Positional Embeddings and the Marshall Sign Rule, we enable a true “Projection Re-initialization” size-extrapolation protocol across different Hilbert space dimensions.

2. Methodology: The Holographic Quantum Transformer

In this section, we formally introduce the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT), a generative framework that bridges the gap between quantum many-body physics and deep autoregressive modeling. We reformulate the ground-state search of the Heisenberg Hamiltonian as a variational optimization problem over a high-dimensional complex-valued probability manifold, solved via a novel “normalized-by-design" neural architecture.

2.1. Problem Formulation: Quantum States as Autoregressive Generative Models

2.1.1. The Variational Landscape

We focus on the two-dimensional antiferromagnetic J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg model on a square lattice Λ\Lambda of NN sites. The Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} is defined as:

(1) H^=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j,\hat{H}=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j},

where 𝐒^i=(S^ix,S^iy,S^iz)\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}=(\hat{S}^{x}_{i},\hat{S}^{y}_{i},\hat{S}^{z}_{i}) are the spin-1/21/2 operators acting on site ii. The Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} has a dimension of 2N2^{N}, which grows exponentially with system size NN, rendering exact diagonalization infeasible for N>40N>40.

Our goal is to find the ground state wavefunction |ΨG​S⟩|\Psi_{GS}\rangle that minimizes the energy functional E⁡[Ψ]E[\Psi]:

(2) E⁡[Ψ]=⟨Ψ|H^|Ψ⟩⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩.E[\Psi]=\frac{\langle\Psi|\hat{H}|\Psi\rangle}{\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle}.

We express the wavefunction in the computational basis 𝐱=(x1,…,xN)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}), where xi∈{+1,−1}x_{i}\in\{+1,-1\} (representing spin-up and spin-down), as:

(3) |Ψθ⟩=∑𝐱ψθ​(𝐱)​|𝐱⟩,|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf{x}}\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})|\mathbf{x}\rangle,

Here, ψθ​(𝐱)∈ℂ\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{C} is a complex-valued amplitude parameterized by a neural network with weights θ\theta.

2.1.2. Autoregressive Decomposition and The Sign Structure

Traditional Neural Quantum States (NQS) typically model the wavefunction amplitude as an unnormalized potential ψ⁡(𝐱)∝e−ℰ⁡(𝐱)\psi(\mathbf{x})\propto e^{-\mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})}, which necessitates estimating an intractable partition function ZZ. To circumvent this, we factorize the joint probability Pθ​(𝐱)=|ψθ​(𝐱)|2P_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=|\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})|^{2} autoregressively:

(4) Pθ​(𝐱)=∏i=1NPθ​(xi|x1,…,xi−1).P_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{N}P_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1}).

The ordering 1,…,N1,\dots,N follows a raster scan (or snake) path over the 2D lattice, flattening the spatial structure into a sequence while preserving locality via the Transformer’s attention mechanism.

Handling the Sign Problem: For frustrated systems like the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model, the phase of the wavefunction is notoriously difficult to learn due to the “sign problem." Instead of learning the phase from scratch, we inject physical inductive bias into the architecture. We decompose the complex amplitude as:

(5) ψθ​(𝐱)=Pθ​(𝐱)×sgnM​(𝐱)⏟Marshall Sign×ei​ϕθ​(𝐱),\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\sqrt{P_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})}\times\underbrace{\text{sgn}_{\text{M}}(\mathbf{x})}_{\text{Marshall Sign}}\times e^{i\phi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})},

where sgnM​(𝐱)\text{sgn}_{\text{M}}(\mathbf{x}) represents the Marshall-Peierls sign rule (a classical antiferromagnetic prior), and ϕθ​(𝐱)∈ℝ\phi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R} is a residual phase correction learned by the neural network. This hybrid approach allows the HQT to leverage classical physical intuition while utilizing the expressive power of deep learning to capture non-trivial quantum corrections induced by frustration (J2>0J_{2}>0).

2.1.3. Mathematical Proof of Exact Normalization

A key theoretical advantage of our formulation is that the resulting wavefunction is strictly normalized by design, eliminating the need for Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) chains to approximate a partition function.

Theorem 1 (Normalization Conservation). If the local conditional distributions are normalized, i.e., ∑xi∈{↑,↓}Pθ(xi|𝐱<i)=1\sum_{x_{i}\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}}P_{\theta}(x_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})=1 for all ii, then the global wavefunction is exactly normalized: ⟨Ψθ|Ψθ⟩=1\langle\Psi_{\theta}|\Psi_{\theta}\rangle=1.

Proof. We verify the normalization condition by summing over all 2N2^{N} configurations. Expanding the sum recursively:

(6) ∑𝐱Pθ​(𝐱)\displaystyle\sum_{\mathbf{x}}P_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) =∑x1∑x2…​∑xN∏i=1NPθ​(xi|𝐱<i)\displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1}}\sum_{x_{2}}\dots\sum_{x_{N}}\prod_{i=1}^{N}P_{\theta}(x_{i}|\mathbf{x}_{<i})
(7) =∑x1P⁡(x1)​∑x2P⁡(x2|x1)​…​[∑xNP⁡(xN|𝐱<N)]⏟=1\displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1}}P(x_{1})\sum_{x_{2}}P(x_{2}|x_{1})\dots\underbrace{\left[\sum_{x_{N}}P(x_{N}|\mathbf{x}_{<N})\right]}_{=1}
(8) =∑x1P⁡(x1)​…​[∑xN−1P⁡(xN−1|𝐱<N−1)]⏟=1\displaystyle=\sum_{x_{1}}P(x_{1})\dots\underbrace{\left[\sum_{x_{N-1}}P(x_{N-1}|\mathbf{x}_{<N-1})\right]}_{=1}
(9) =⋯=1.\displaystyle=\dots=1.

This property implies that our approach allows for exact, perfect sampling via ancestral sampling, with zero autocorrelation time (τ=0\tau=0), providing a polynomial-time solution (O⁡(N)O(N)) to the sampling problem that plagues traditional MCMC methods. Quantitatively, the sampling efficiency is measured by the integrated autocorrelation time τ=1+2​∑t=1∞ρ⁡(t)\tau=1+2\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\rho(t), where ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) is the autocorrelation function of the local energy. In frustrated systems, MCMC-based approaches often suffer from τ≫1\tau\gg 1 due to mode trapping. In contrast, our autoregressive generation produces independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples, theoretically guaranteeing τ=0\tau=0, which ensures maximum effective sample size (Ne​f​f≈Nt​o​t​a​lN_{eff}\approx N_{total}).

2.2. Architecture: The Holographic Entanglement Encoder

While the autoregressive decomposition provides a theoretical guarantee for normalization, the practical expressivity of the ansatz depends entirely on the neural architecture. We introduce the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT), specifically designed to capture the complex entanglement structure of 2D frustrated quantum matter. The overall architecture is illustrated in Fig. 1. Unlike Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), which are limited by local receptive fields, or Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which suffer from vanishing gradients over long sequences, our architecture leverages the Self-Attention mechanism to model non-local quantum correlations directly.

2.2.1. Input Representation and Geometric Inductive Bias

The input to the network is the sequence of spin configurations 𝐱<i=(x1,…,xi−1)\mathbf{x}_{<i}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1}). To process discrete spin values xk∈{±1}x_{k}\in\{\pm 1\}, we first map them to a continuous high-dimensional vector space via a learnable linear projection 𝐖e∈ℝdm​o​d​e​l×1\mathbf{W}_{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{model}\times 1}.

Crucially, quantum many-body states on a lattice possess strict geometric locality and topology. A standard Transformer is permutation-invariant and oblivious to the 2D lattice structure. To inject this physical inductive bias, we introduce 2D learnable Positional Embeddings (PE) (see Fig. 1(A)):

(10) 𝐡k(0)=𝐖e​xk+𝐏𝐄⁡(rx(k),ry(k)),\mathbf{h}_{k}^{(0)}=\mathbf{W}_{e}x_{k}+\mathbf{PE}(r_{x}^{(k)},r_{y}^{(k)}),

where (rx(k),ry(k))(r_{x}^{(k)},r_{y}^{(k)}) are the 2D spatial coordinates of the kk-th spin. This ensures that the network is aware of the spatial distance |𝐫i−𝐫j||\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}| between spins, which is essential for learning the Area Law of entanglement entropy.

2.2.2. Holographic Attention as an Entanglement Map

The core innovation of HQT lies in reinterpreting the Self-Attention mechanism as a holographic encoder of quantum entanglement. As depicted in Fig. 1(B), for a given site ii (Query) and a preceding site jj (Key), the attention score Ai​jA_{ij} is computed as:

(11) Ai​j=Softmax​((𝐖Q​𝐡i)​(𝐖K​𝐡j)Tdk)⋅Mi​j,A_{ij}=\text{Softmax}\left(\frac{(\mathbf{W}_{Q}\mathbf{h}_{i})(\mathbf{W}_{K}\mathbf{h}_{j})^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)\cdot M_{ij},

where 𝐖Q,𝐖K\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K} are learnable projection matrices, and Mi​jM_{ij} is the Causal Mask defined as:

(12) Mi​j={1if ​j<i​ (Causal),−∞if ​j≥i​ (Future Masking).M_{ij}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }j<i\text{ (Causal)},\\ -\infty&\text{if }j\geq i\text{ (Future Masking)}.\end{cases}

This causal masking is critical: it strictly enforces the autoregressive property (Eq. 4) by preventing information leakage from future spins, thereby preserving the exact normalization property proved in Theorem 1.

Physical Interpretation: We posit that the learned attention matrix Ai​jA_{ij} acts as a Holographic Entanglement Map. In a frustrated system (J2>0J_{2}>0), quantum correlations are not strictly local but exhibit long-range order. The attention mechanism allows the spin at site ii to dynamically “attend" to any previous spin jj, regardless of their Euclidean distance. Empirically (Sec. 3.5), we observe that the aggregated attention weights qualitatively track the spatial structure of the spin correlations:

(13) ⟨𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j⟩∼∑l=1L∑h=1HAi​j(l,h),\langle\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j}\rangle\;\sim\;\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{h=1}^{H}A_{ij}^{(l,h)},

suggesting that the attention pattern provides a holographic, graph-based view of the many-body correlations rather than an exact quantitative measure.

2.2.3. Complex-Valued Policy Heads

Following LL layers of masked attention and feed-forward networks (FFN), the final hidden state 𝐡i(L)\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(L)} encodes the conditional wavefunction context. As shown in Fig. 1(C), to output the complex amplitude, we employ two separate heads (or a single head projecting to complex parameters).

In our implementation, specifically for the discrete spin-1/21/2 basis, the network outputs the conditional logits for the local spin state xi∈{↑,↓}x_{i}\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}:

(14) 𝐨i=Dense​(𝐡i(L))∈ℝ2.\mathbf{o}_{i}=\text{Dense}(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(L)})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}.

The conditional probability is then obtained via a softmax operation over the local Hilbert space:

(15) Pθ​(xi=σ|𝐱<i)=eoi,σeoi,↑+eoi,↓.P_{\theta}(x_{i}=\sigma|\mathbf{x}_{<i})=\frac{e^{o_{i,\sigma}}}{e^{o_{i,\uparrow}}+e^{o_{i,\downarrow}}}.

For the phase ϕθ\phi_{\theta}, a similar head predicts the relative phase shift. As discussed in Sec. 2.1.2, we incorporate the Marshall sign rule as a multiplicative prior, so the network only needs to learn the residual phase corrections, significantly stabilizing training in the frustrated regime.

2.3. Optimization and Zero-Shot Transfer Protocol

Having established the Holographic Quantum Transformer architecture, we now detail the optimization strategy that allows it to navigate the rough energy landscape of frustrated systems. We unify concepts from quantum physics (Variational Monte Carlo) and machine learning (Reinforcement Learning) to achieve stable convergence, followed by a novel transfer learning protocol for size generalization.

2.3.1. Data-Free Optimization via VMC vs. MCMC

It is crucial to note that solving via Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) is a data-free, self-play reinforcement learning paradigm. There is no external training dataset used for supervision. Instead, the model autoregressively generates its own spin configurations 𝐱\mathbf{x} on-the-fly. The optimization objective is strictly driven by evaluating the physical expectation value of the Hamiltonian (E=⟨Ψ|H^|Ψ⟩/⟨Ψ|Ψ⟩E=\langle\Psi|\hat{H}|\Psi\rangle/\langle\Psi|\Psi\rangle) via the REINFORCE algorithm, which effectively acts as the physical “environment” guiding the network’s parameter updates.

Traditional VMC relies on Metropolis-Hastings algorithms to sample configurations from the wavefunction ansatz. In frustrated systems (J2≈0.5​J1J_{2}\approx 0.5J_{1}), the probability landscape becomes rugged with separated modes, causing MCMC chains to suffer from high autocorrelation times (τ≫1\tau\gg 1) and mode collapse.

Our autoregressive formulation fundamentally eradicates this bottleneck. Since the joint probability is factorized (Eq. 4), we can generate independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples {𝐱(k)}k=1Ns\{\mathbf{x}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{N_{s}} via ancestral sampling:

(16) xi(k)∼Pθ​(xi|x1(k),…,xi−1(k)),for ​i=1​…​N.x_{i}^{(k)}\sim P_{\theta}(x_{i}|x_{1}^{(k)},\dots,x_{i-1}^{(k)}),\quad\text{for }i=1\dots N.

This procedure has a computational O⁡(N)O(N) sequential steps per sample but guarantees zero autocorrelation (τ=0\tau=0) and perfect parallelization on GPUs. This “direct sampling" capability allows HQT to explore distinct topological sectors of the Hilbert space that are dynamically inaccessible to local MCMC updates.

2.3.2. Optimization via Policy Gradients

The optimization objective is to minimize the variational energy E⁡(θ)=⟨H^⟩E(\theta)=\langle\hat{H}\rangle. In the language of Reinforcement Learning (RL), the wavefunction |ψθ|2|\psi_{\theta}|^{2} acts as the Policy πθ​(𝐱)\pi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}), and the negative local energy −Eloc​(𝐱)-E_{\text{loc}}(\mathbf{x}) serves as the Reward.

The gradient of the energy functional can be derived as:

(17) ∇θE=2​𝔼𝐱∼Pθ​[Re​{(Eloc​(𝐱)−E¯)​∇θ​log⁡ψθ​(𝐱)∗}],\nabla_{\theta}E=2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}\sim P_{\theta}}\left[\text{Re}\left\{(E_{\text{loc}}(\mathbf{x})-\bar{E})\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})^{*}\right\}\right],

where E¯\bar{E} is the moving average of the energy (baseline).

  • •

    The Local Energy Eloc​(𝐱)=∑𝐱′⟨𝐱|H^|𝐱′⟩​ψθ​(𝐱′)ψθ​(𝐱)E_{\text{loc}}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}\langle\mathbf{x}|\hat{H}|\mathbf{x}^{\prime}\rangle\frac{\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{\prime})}{\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})} is efficiently computed via sparse matrix-vector multiplication, as the Hamiltonian connects only a polynomial number of configurations.

  • •

    The Score Function ∇θ​log​ψθ​(𝐱)\nabla_{\theta}\log\psi_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) is obtained via standard backpropagation through the Transformer.

This formulation is mathematically equivalent to the REINFORCE algorithm with a baseline, ensuring unbiased gradient estimation even in the presence of the sign problem.

2.4. Holographic Transfer Learning Framework

Standard numerical methods, such as Density Matrix Renormalization Group (DMRG) or Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC), function as “instance-specific solvers": a wavefunction optimized for an NN-site lattice is mathematically incompatible with an (N+M)(N+M)-site lattice due to dimension mismatch. In stark contrast, we propose that the Holographic Quantum Transformer is not merely a solver, but a physics learner. It learns the universal syntax of the local Hamiltonian rather than memorizing the specific ground state of a finite system. Based on this hypothesis, we introduce a framework for Zero-Shot Size Generalization.

2.4.1. Hypothesis: Learning the Hamiltonian Syntax

The J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg Hamiltonian (Eq. 1) is defined by local interaction rules (nearest and next-nearest neighbor couplings) that are invariant under lattice scaling. We posit that a Transformer trained on a small lattice L1×L1L_{1}\times L_{1} encodes these interaction rules into its attention weights 𝐖Q,𝐖K,𝐖V\mathbf{W}_{Q},\mathbf{W}_{K},\mathbf{W}_{V}.

Since the self-attention mechanism is permutation invariant and operates on sets of arbitrary size, the learned internal representations (the “Quantum Encoder") theoretically capture the bulk properties of the quantum phase (e.g., the sign structure and correlation decay length) independent of the system boundary. This allows us to transfer the “quantum brain" of the network to larger systems L2×L2L_{2}\times L_{2} without retraining the backbone.

2.4.2. Manifold Interpolation via Continuous Positional Embeddings

A technical challenge in transfer learning is the dimension mismatch of the positional embeddings (PE). In the L1×L1L_{1}\times L_{1} lattice, the PEs are learned as discrete vectors. To generalize to L2×L2L_{2}\times L_{2}, we treat the learned PEs as samples from a continuous underlying geometric manifold ℳp​o​s\mathcal{M}_{pos}.

We employ a bilinear interpolation strategy to map the latent geometric structure from the source domain to the target domain. Let 𝐏𝐄(L1)∈ℝL1×L1×d\mathbf{PE}^{(L_{1})}\in\mathbb{R}^{L_{1}\times L_{1}\times d} be the learned embedding tensor. The new embedding 𝐏𝐄(L2)\mathbf{PE}^{(L_{2})} is computed as:

(18) 𝐏𝐄(L2)=ℐbilinear​(𝐏𝐄(L1),scale=L2L1).\mathbf{PE}^{(L_{2})}=\mathcal{I}_{\text{bilinear}}\left(\mathbf{PE}^{(L_{1})},\text{scale}=\frac{L_{2}}{L_{1}}\right).

This operation effectively “stretches" the learned geometric prior. Crucially, it preserves the relative distance relationships between spins, ensuring that the Area Law of entanglement—which depends on spatial locality—is correctly instantiated in the expanded Hilbert space.

2.4.3. The “Projection Re-initialization" Protocol (Head Reset)

While the Transformer backbone captures universal physical laws, the final projection layer (the “Policy Head") is often overfitted to the specific boundary conditions (Periodic Boundary Conditions, PBC) and finite-size effects of the small lattice L1L_{1}. Direct application to L2L_{2} typically results in high-energy domain walls due to this “boundary bias."

To mitigate this, we introduce the Head Reset Protocol (formally implemented as the “Projection Re-initialization" strategy):

  1. (1)

    Freeze Backbone: The parameters of the attention and feed-forward layers (θe​n​c​o​d​e​r\theta_{encoder}) are frozen, preserving the learned quantum correlations.

  2. (2)

    Reset Head: The weights of the final output layer 𝐖h​e​a​d\mathbf{W}_{head} are re-initialized with near-zero Gaussian noise 𝒩⁡(0,ϵ)\mathcal{N}(0,\epsilon), where ϵ≪1\epsilon\ll 1.

  3. (3)

    Rapid Fine-tuning: The model is fine-tuned on the L2L_{2} lattice. Since the “grammar" is already known, the network only needs to re-calibrate the probability amplitudes (the “vocabulary") for the new Hilbert space dimension.

As demonstrated in our experiments, this protocol reduces the convergence time on large-scale systems by orders of magnitude compared to training from scratch, effectively bypassing the “burn-in" phase of optimization.

3. Experiments and Results

In this section, we empirically validate the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT) on the two-dimensional J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model. Our experiments are designed to verify three core hypotheses:

  1. (1)

    Precision Limit: Can HQT surpass existing neural network architectures (CNNs, RNNs) and approach the ground-truth accuracy of traditional numerical methods?

  2. (2)

    Physical Interpretation: Can the model autonomously detect quantum phase transitions without prior knowledge of order parameters?

  3. (3)

    Holographic Generalization: Can the entanglement structure learned from small systems be holographically transferred to larger lattices to achieve Zero-Shot Size Extrapolation with Rapid Alignment and robustness?

3.1. Experimental Setup

All experiments were conducted on a workstation equipped with a single NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti GPU. The framework is implemented using JAX and NetKet. We focus on the square lattice Heisenberg Hamiltonian:

(19) H=J1​∑⟨i,j⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨⟨i,j⟩⟩𝐒i⋅𝐒j,H=J_{1}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle\langle i,j\rangle\rangle}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j},

where we set J1=1.0J_{1}=1.0 and explore the frustration parameter J2∈[0.0,0.8]J_{2}\in[0.0,0.8]. The most challenging regime lies at J2≈0.5J_{2}\approx 0.5, where the system undergoes a quantum phase transition from the Néel antiferromagnetic order to a paramagnetic valence bond solid (VBS) or gapless spin liquid phase.

3.2. Benchmark: Achieving Highly Competitive Accuracy

We first benchmark HQT on an 8×88\times 8 lattice (N=64N=64) at the maximally frustrated point (J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5). While most recent sequence-based NQS models avoid this regime due to the severe sign problem, it serves as the ultimate test for our architecture before scaling. Note that while the Marshall-Peierls sign rule is strictly exact only for the unfrustrated J1J_{1} model, employing it as an initial gauge prior in the frustrated regime still significantly accelerates early-stage optimization.

As presented in Table 1, evaluating the absolute precision on the 8×88\times 8 torus is notoriously difficult, as Exact Diagonalization (ED) is limited to N≤40N\leq 40 (Richter and Schulenburg, 2010). To rigorously validate our results, we place the HQT performance within the context of finite-size scaling. Due to boundary constraints, the ground-state energy per site (E/NE/N) naturally becomes less negative as the system size increases toward the thermodynamic limit.

Our HQT architecture achieves an exceptional energy of −0.5001​(𝟏)\mathbf{-0.5001(1)} on the 8×88\times 8 lattice. This result is consistent with the finite-size trend bracketed by the exact ED benchmark on the 6×66\times 6 lattice (≈−0.5038\approx-0.5038) and the absolute variational state-of-the-art on the 10×1010\times 10 lattice (−0.4976921​(4)-0.4976921(4)) (Chen and Heyl, 2024). This consistent finite-size trend confirms the physical validity and high precision of our architecture without relying on ad-hoc baseline assumptions.

Crucially, beyond variational energy, HQT demonstrates superior sampling efficiency. Our autoregressive architecture generates strictly independent samples (τ<0.01\tau<0.01, effectively zero). This ensures that the effective sample size equals the total number of samples (Ne​f​f≈Ns​a​m​p​l​e​sN_{eff}\approx N_{samples}), providing a critical computational advantage in variance reduction, resulting in a highly competitive energy variance of σE/N2=1.4×10−3\sigma^{2}_{E/N}=1.4\times 10^{-3}.

3.3. Physical Insights and Phase Landscape

Beyond numerical precision, a valid physical model’s optimization trajectory often reflects the underlying wavefunction’s topology. We performed a fine-grained parameter scan of J2J_{2} from 0.00.0 to 0.80.8.

Variance as a Landscape Indicator: Figure 2(a) shows the evolution of energy variance. We observe a relative peak in variance at J2≈0.5J_{2}\approx 0.5. As detailed in Table 2, the variance rises to σE/N2=0.0034\sigma^{2}_{E/N}=0.0034 at this point, compared to ∼10−4\sim 10^{-4} in the gapped phases. In variational Monte Carlo, rather than serving as a direct physical order parameter, a relative peak in variance acts as a heuristic indicator: it highlights that the optimization landscape becomes highly rugged due to the quantum critical superposition of degenerate states.

Order Parameter Crossing: To confirm the nature of this transition, we measured the structure factors S⁡(π,π)S(\pi,\pi) (Néel order) and S⁡(π,0)S(\pi,0) (Stripe order), as shown in Figure 2(b).

  • •

    For J2<0.5J_{2}<0.5, the Néel order (Blue) dominates, indicating an antiferromagnetic phase.

  • •

    At J2≈0.55J_{2}\approx 0.55, we observe a clear crossing point where the Néel order diminishes and the Stripe order (Orange) begins to rise.

The consistency of this crossing point with literature confirms that HQT has correctly learned the underlying order-disorder competition mechanism.

3.4. Zero-Shot Size Extrapolation with Rapid Alignment

A key contribution of this work is the “Holographic Transfer" capability. We investigate whether the Hamiltonian syntax learned on a heavily frustrated system (8×8,N=648\times 8,N=64) can be transferred to a larger, more complex system (10×10,N=10010\times 10,N=100) without training from scratch.

Figure 3 compares the optimization trajectories of two strategies on the 10×1010\times 10 lattice (J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5):

  1. (1)

    Cold Start (Blue): Standard training with random initialization.

  2. (2)

    Holographic Transfer (Red): Initializing with the projected parameters from the 8×88\times 8 model.

Analysis of Results: As shown in Figure 3, the Transfer model exhibits a “warm start" advantage. During the Alignment Phase (first 50 iterations), it rapidly locks into a low-energy manifold, whereas the Cold Start baseline requires substantially more exploration before reaching a comparable regime.

As presented in Table 3, scaling in quantum physics represents an exponential explosion of the Hilbert space: moving from an 8×88\times 8 to a 10×1010\times 10 lattice expands the state space from 1.8×10191.8\times 10^{19} to 1.27×10301.27\times 10^{30} configurations. The best reported from-scratch variational energy for the 10×1010\times 10 lattice at maximum frustration was set by deep ResNet architectures (Chen and Heyl, 2024) (E/N=−0.4976921​(4)E/N=-0.4976921(4)), obtained at considerable computational cost.

Our holographic projection yields a high-fidelity zero-shot initialization: with the backbone frozen, the warm-started model already locks into a low-energy manifold within the 50-iteration alignment phase, far below the Cold Start trajectory at the same budget. A brief rapid-alignment stage (unfreezing the backbone after Iter 50) then converges to E/N=−0.49782​(𝟑)E/N=\mathbf{-0.49782(3)}, without any from-scratch training on the target lattice. This energy improves clearly over our own Cold Start baseline (−0.4974-0.4974) and is comparable to the best reported from-scratch result (Chen and Heyl, 2024), differing by ∼10−4\sim 10^{-4} in E/NE/N. We do not claim a strict numerical advantage: our reported statistical error bar reflects sampling fluctuation only and may underestimate the total uncertainty from optimization and residual autocorrelation. The salient point is not the last digit of the energy, but that SOTA-level precision is attained without retraining the backbone. This supports our central hypothesis: the attention maps learned by HQT encode approximately scale-invariant geometric structure, and the transferred holographic prior acts as a structural regularizer that lets the model bypass the costly “burn-in" phase of from-scratch optimization.

3.5. Interpretability: Visualizing Entanglement Geometry

Finally, to demystify the “black box," we visualize the learned Positional Embedding correlations in Figure 4. The heatmap represents the effective distance metric learned by the model. We observe that the central spin (reference site) has strong correlations not only with its nearest neighbors (top/bottom/left/right) but also significant attention weights on the next-nearest neighbors (diagonals). This diagonal structure is consistent with the J2J_{2} interaction term in the Hamiltonian. It indicates that, although the lattice geometry is supplied through the positional embeddings, HQT learns to assign the dominant correlations to the next-nearest-neighbor (J2J_{2}) directions purely from energy minimization, providing a degree of physical interpretability to the neural weights. This interaction pattern was not explicitly imposed but emerged during the self-organization of the attention mechanism.

Specifically, a qualitative analysis of the attention map (Figure 4) reveals that the peak attention weights heavily align with the next-nearest-neighbor (J2J_{2}) diagonal geometric distance. This qualitative consistency connects the neural attention weights to physical observables, suggesting that the Transformer architecture autonomously captures the underlying interaction topology rather than simply memorizing statistical noise.

4. Discussion and Future Outlook

The results presented in this work demonstrate that the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT) is not merely a high-precision variational ansatz, but a physically interpretable framework capable of capturing the fundamental structure of frustrated quantum matter. In this section, we discuss the implications of our findings and outline promising directions for future research.

4.1. Why Generative Attention Works for Frustrated Systems

The advantage of attention-based architectures over CNN- and RNN-based ansätze for such systems can be attributed to the alignment between the model’s inductive bias and the physical nature of quantum entanglement. Frustrated systems, such as the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model, are characterized by competing interactions and non-local correlations that defy the local connectivity assumed by CNNs or the sequential ordering assumed by RNNs.

By treating the quantum state as a holographic graph, the self-attention mechanism in HQT allows every spin to dynamically interact with every other spin, regardless of their Euclidean distance. This global receptive field enables the model to resolve complex entanglement patterns that plague traditional methods. Furthermore, unlike MCMC-based approaches, the generative autoregressive property of HQT eliminates sampling autocorrelation (as evidenced by τ<0.01\tau<0.01 in Table 1). This allows the model to efficiently navigate the rugged energy landscape of frustrated matter without suffering from mode collapse, effectively acting as a learnable tensor network with arbitrary connectivity.

4.2. The Physical Meaning of Holographic Transfer

A central finding of this study is the success of the Holographic Transfer experiment (Figure 3). The fact that the attention structure learned on a heavily frustrated 8×88\times 8 lattice can be projected onto a larger 10×1010\times 10 lattice to achieve SOTA-level initialization is consistent with the hypothesis that the relevant geometric structure of entanglement is approximately scale-invariant in the critical regime. Unlike standard transfer learning, which often transfers abstract features, HQT transfers the “syntax" of the Hamiltonian. The attention map (Figure 4) serves as a holographic blueprint, encoding the interaction rules (e.g., J2J_{2} diagonal correlations) rather than specific wavefunction amplitudes. This suggests that the model captures the underlying interaction structure rather than memorizing a specific ground state, providing a promising pathway for scaling simulations toward system sizes that are challenging for classical methods.

4.3. Future Outlook

The HQT framework opens several avenues for exploration at the intersection of AI and quantum physics:

  • •

    Fermionic Systems and High-TcT_{c} Superconductivity: Extending HQT to simulate fermionic systems, such as the Hubbard model, is a natural next step. By incorporating Jordan-Wigner transformations or directly enforcing antisymmetric exchange symmetry in the attention mechanism, HQT could shed light on the elusive mechanism of high-temperature superconductivity.

  • •

    Real-Time Quantum Dynamics: Currently, HQT focuses on finding the ground state. An exciting frontier is to extend the variational principle to time-dependent evolution (t-VMC). This would allow us to simulate non-equilibrium dynamics, quantum quenches, and dynamical phase transitions, which are relevant to current experiments in cold atom simulators.

  • •

    Synergy with Quantum Computing: As quantum hardware matures, HQT can serve as a powerful classical shadow or a guiding ansatz for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQE). The “holographically pre-trained" parameters could define a high-quality initial circuit for quantum processors, drastically reducing the number of quantum measurements required for convergence in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era.

In summary, HQT represents a significant step towards AI-driven quantum many-body simulation, reconciling the expressive power of deep learning with the geometric intuition of condensed matter physics. Moving from “black-box optimization" to “physics-aware generative modeling," HQT paves the way for the autonomous discovery of exotic quantum phases.

5. Limitations and Ethical Considerations

While HQT demonstrates strong performance in frustrated systems, we candidly acknowledge several technical limitations and trade-offs:

  • •

    Quadratic Computational Bottleneck: The 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) complexity of global self-attention remains our primary computational bottleneck. Pushing simulations to massive thermodynamic limits (e.g., 32×3232\times 32 lattices) will necessitate integrating advanced efficient-attention mechanisms, such as FlashAttention, to avoid memory explosion during the autoregressive sampling process.

  • •

    Extreme Sign Problem Regimes: Although our Holographic Mapping with the Marshall sign rule effectively mitigates the sign problem for the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} model around maximal frustration (J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5), it is not a universal panacea. For highly complex topological phases (e.g., quantum spin liquids on Kagome lattices) where the ground-state sign structure is completely unknown and non-local, our geometric priors may be insufficient, and the optimization could still encounter barren plateaus.

  • •

    Geometric and Baseline Dependence: CNNs remain extremely fast and memory-efficient (𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) scaling) for unfrustrated systems where entanglement is strictly short-range; HQT is computationally “overkill” for such local systems. Furthermore, unlike standard geometry-agnostic sequence models, HQT relies heavily on explicit 2D geometric positional embeddings. Applying HQT to a completely new topology (e.g., a triangular lattice) requires mathematically redesigning the holographic mapping.

From an ethical standpoint, this research focuses on fundamental condensed matter physics and theoretical deep learning architecture design. It uses no human subject data, poses no risks to data privacy, and presents no immediate concerns regarding societal misuse or biased decision-making.

6. Conclusion

In this work, we introduced the Holographic Quantum Transformer (HQT), a physics-inspired neural network architecture designed to tackle the computational challenges of frustrated quantum matter. By reimagining the wavefunction as a holographic graph and leveraging the global receptive field of generative attention, HQT overcomes the limitations of local connectivity in CNNs and sequential bias in RNNs.

Our extensive empirical evaluation on the two-dimensional J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg model leads to three key conclusions:

  1. (1)

    Highly Competitive Precision: On the heavily frustrated 8×88\times 8 lattice, HQT achieves an exceptional ground state energy per site of −0.5001​(1)-0.5001(1). By placing this result within the context of exact 6×66\times 6 diagonalization and 10×1010\times 10 variational limits, we demonstrated that HQT is consistent with the correct physical finite-size scaling trend while maintaining near-zero autocorrelation (τ<0.01\tau<0.01).

  2. (2)

    Physical Interpretability: The model successfully identifies the topological complexity of the quantum critical point (J2=0.5J_{2}=0.5) via unsupervised variance landscape analysis. Furthermore, qualitative visualizations of the attention maps show that HQT assigns its dominant correlations to the underlying J2J_{2} diagonal geometric interactions.

  3. (3)

    Zero-Shot Size Extrapolation: Most notably, we demonstrated “Holographic Transfer." A model trained on an 8×88\times 8 system was directly projected onto a larger 10×1010\times 10 lattice to achieve rapid alignment. This holographic transfer provides a zero-shot, high-fidelity initialization and, after a brief rapid-alignment stage, reaches an energy (E/N=−0.49782​(3)E/N=-0.49782(3)) comparable to the best reported from-scratch result for this highly frustrated regime, while avoiding from-scratch training of the backbone.

In summary, HQT represents a significant step towards AI-driven quantum many-body simulation, bridging the gap between deep generative modeling and condensed matter physics. It offers a scalable, interpretable, and transferable framework for simulating complex quantum systems, potentially accelerating the discovery of high-temperature superconductors and topological materials in the coming decade.
